questions.q: What problem do BULK COLLECT and FORALL exist to solve?
options: The overhead of repeated context switches between the PL/SQL engine and the SQL engine during row-by-row processing
The inability to declare variables inside a loop
The lack of an EXCEPTION section in cursor loops
The inability to use associative arrays inside a FOR loop
questions.explain: Every fetch or DML statement in a row-by-row cursor loop triggers a context switch; BULK COLLECT and FORALL collapse many of those into one.

questions.q: What does SELECT ... BULK COLLECT INTO do?
options: Fetches an entire result set into a collection in a single context switch
Runs an UPDATE across every row of a collection in one operation
Converts a cursor into a REF CURSOR automatically
Commits the current transaction before fetching
questions.explain: BULK COLLECT fetches ALL matching rows into a collection at once, instead of one row per context switch.

options: Sends a batch of INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE statements across a whole collection as one bulk DML operation
Fetches a result set row by row with extra logging
Declares a new collection type
Replaces the need for a DECLARE section entirely
questions.explain: FORALL executes one DML statement per collection element but sends them all to the SQL engine as a single bulk operation, not a loop of individual statements.

questions.q: What is the overall technique of combining BULK COLLECT and FORALL called?
options: Bulk binding
Autonomous transaction binding
Context collapsing
Pipeline bulking
questions.explain: Bulk binding is a well-known, well-documented real Oracle PL/SQL performance recommendation, not an obscure trick.

questions.q: What T-SQL habit does BULK COLLECT/FORALL parallel?
options: Preferring a set-based INSERT...SELECT or table-valued parameter over looping through rows one at a time with a cursor
Preferring TRY...CATCH over an EXCEPTION section
Always using a table variable instead of a temp table
Avoiding stored procedures entirely in favor of ad hoc batches
questions.explain: Both reflect the same underlying lesson: minimize round trips between the procedural layer and the SQL engine, whichever platform you're on.
